definition: Head of a monastic order or spiritual community. An Acharya has attained the highest level of spiritual scholarship and self-discipline and is authorized to teach and initiate disciples.
Non-destructive karmas that obscure the soul's power, feeling, body, and lifespan but do not destroy its nature. The four aghatiya karmas are Vedaniya, Nama, Gotra, and Ayu.
Non-sentient substance; one of the 6 fundamental realities. Includes Pudgala (matter), Dharma (medium of motion), Adharma (medium of rest), Akasha (space), and Kala (time).
Infinite knowledge possessed by Kevalis (omniscient beings) who have destroyed all knowledge-obscuring karma.
The 12 small vows for laypersons, creating a gradual path toward liberation while managing worldly duties. Derived from the Mahavratas but adapted for householder life.
Non-possession — the third of the Mahavratas. Not merely limiting material goods but completely detaching the heart from desire and accumulation.
Devotional ritual of waving a lit lamp before the Tirthankara idol while singing hymns. Can also be performed before a sacred book or Guru's feet.
The mantra 'Aim Hrim Klim' used as a devotional seed-syllable mantra for invoking Arihant energy. Used in meditation and mantra-sadhana.
Any substance that has spatial extension (body). Jiva and the four main Ajiva dravyas are Astikaya; Kala (time) is not.
Bondage of karma to the soul, determined by the strength of passions (kashaya) and the intensity of action at the moment of action.
Contemplative meditation on spiritual themes such as the impermanence of all things, the solitariness of the soul, and the futility of worldly attachments.
Celibacy or complete control of sexual energy — the fourth Mahavrata for monks and a graduated vow for householders.

A universal monarch who rules over the entire world. Several Chakravartins appear in Jain tradition, including Bharata (son of Rishabhdev). They are as powerful as Tirthankaras but do not attain liberation through their rule.
The four-month rainy season when monks stay at one place to avoid harming life. A period of intensified practice, study, and community.
Charity or giving — one of the fourfold pillars of Jain practice. Includes giving food, medicine, shelter, and knowledge to those in need.
One of the two major Jain sects whose monks practice complete nudity as the highest expression of non-possession.
Meditation — concentrated mental focus on a spiritual object. In Jainism, only Dharma Dhyana and Shukla Dhyana lead to liberation.
Substance or matter; one of the seven categories of reality in Jain metaphysics.
The four states of existence: Deva (heavenly), Manushya (human), Tiryanca (animal/plant), and Naraki (hellish). Souls transmigrate through these states based on karma.
Lineage or family karma determining birth in high or low social status across lifetimes.
The 14 stages of spiritual progress from complete delusion to final liberation. Each stage represents increasingly purified consciousness.
Spiritual teacher; in Jainism usually refers to the Acharya or Upadhyaya who imparts scriptural knowledge and guides disciples toward liberation.
Conqueror — one who has conquered the inner enemies (passions, attachment, aversion). Tirthankaras are also called Jinas; followers are called Jains.
The sentient soul — infinite in number, eternal, and the central actor in the drama of liberation. Every Jiva has the potential for infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and power.
Time — the dimension of change. In Jain cosmology, time is cyclical, consisting of ascending (Utsarpini) and descending (Avasarpini) half-cycles.
Passions — the four sticky karmic substances (anger, pride, deceit, greed) that cause karmic bandha and keep the soul in samsara.
Omniscience — infinite knowledge attained after destroying all four Ghatiya karmas. The state of a Tirthankara or Arihant before final Nirvana.
The annual day of universal forgiveness (Samvatsari) when Jains seek and grant forgiveness to all beings for harm caused during the past year.
The universe in Jain cosmology, shaped like a figure-eight or a man standing with arms akimbo. Three realms exist within it: upper (heavenly), middle (human/animal), and lower (hellish).
The middle world of Jain cosmology where humans, animals, and plants reside. It consists of Jambudvipa and surrounding continents and oceans.
The five great vows of absolute non-violence, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession, observed by monks and nuns.
Universal friendlessness — one of the 4 forms of meditation, developing unconditional goodwill toward all beings. Opposite of hatred.
The 14 investigative categories used to examine the soul's qualities. The soul evolves through Marganas toward higher Gunasthanaks.
Liberation — final release from all karmic bondage. The soul rises to Siddhashila, infinite in knowledge, perception, bliss, and power.
The path to liberation — the combined practice of Right Faith, Right Knowledge, and Right Conduct (Ratnatraya).
A Jain monk who has taken the Mahavratas. Muni reside in the middle world and practice severe austerities.
The general or common viewpoint — one of the 7 standpoints (Nayas) used in Jain logic to understand partial aspects of truth.

Microscopic, one-sensed beings that exist in vast colonies in earth, air, water, and fire. They represent the lowest form of life in the soul's journey. Jains avoid harming them through boiling water, using filters, etc.
Shedding of karma — the process of destroying karmic matter through austerities, penance, and meditation before it bears fruit.
The act of surrendering everything at the Guru's feet — a formal ritual symbolizing complete renunciation of the world.
Karma that obstructs the soul's energy, preventing charitable acts, spiritual gain, and enjoyment. Destroyed through generosity and equanimity.
The five supreme beings whom Jains venerate: Arihant, Siddha, Acharya, Upadhyaya, and Sadhu. The Navkar Mantra bows to each in sequence.
A pandit of Jainism — a scholar who has mastered the texts, rituals, and philosophy. Often a householder who serves as a religious leader and educator.
The 8-day (Svetambara) or 10-day (Digambara) festival of self-purification. The most sacred time in the Jain calendar, culminating in Samvatsari (universal forgiveness).
The 10th day of the month of Paush, celebrating the birth of Lord Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara.
The ancient language of the Jain Agamas. Many canonical texts are composed in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, the Magadhi dialect of ancient India.
The 11 stages or steps of spiritual practice for lay Jains, preparing them for monastic life. Each Pratima represents a deeper vow and practice.
Religious teacher in Jainism who imparts spiritual wisdom and guides disciples on the path of liberation.
The dravya (substance) of matter in Jainism — the only substance that is tangible, has color, smell, taste, and touch, and combines into atoms and molecules.
The 14 ancient canonical texts of the Digambara tradition that are now lost but were known to Acharya Bhadrabahu. They contained the most esoteric philosophical and cosmological knowledge.
The Three Jewels of Jainism: Right Faith, Right Knowledge, Right Conduct. Together they form the path to liberation.
The first Tirthankara of the current age. Also called Adinath. He taught civilization to humanity — agriculture, arts, governance, and the path of liberation.
A Jain ascetic or monk who has renounced the world and observes the Mahavratas.
Voluntary, gradual fasting to death at the end of life, practiced with full equanimity and Guru approval. The supreme vow of spiritual peace.
One who practices Sallekhana. Only undertaken when death is imminent and with complete spiritual preparation.
Carefulness — the 5 Samitis are carefulness in walking, speaking, eating, placing objects, and disposing of waste. They stop karmic influx.
Stoppage — the process of preventing new karmic influx through vows, carefulness, and spiritual practices.
The four-fold Jain community: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. The Sangha preserves and propagates the teachings.
A Svetambara sub-sect that worships in simple halls (Sthanakas) without idols, focusing on meditation on the pure self.
A thread or aphorism — concise scripture forming the basis of Jain literature. The Agamas are collections of Sutras.
One of the two major Jain sects whose monks wear white robes as an expression of practical non-possession.
Austerity — the 12 forms of self-discipline (6 external, 6 internal) that destroy karma and accelerate spiritual progress.
The 7 fundamental principles of reality: Jiva, Ajiva, Asrava, Bandha, Samvara, Nirjara, Moksha.
A reform movement within Digambara and Svetambara traditions that rejects idol worship and emphasizes simple ethical practice and study.
A sacred pilgrimage site established by a Tirthankara. There are four main Tirthas: Sammed Shikharji, Palitana, Girnar, and Pawapuri.
A ford-maker — a soul who has attained Kevala Jnana and established the four-fold Sangha. There are 24 Tirthankaras in each half-cycle of time.
A learned monk-teacher who instructs other monks and nuns in the scriptures and philosophy. Below Acharya in rank.
A lay follower or householder who observes the 12 Anuvratas and practices Jain Dharma while living in the world.
Detachment or renunciation — the mental state of being free from attachment to worldly objects, relationships, and outcomes.
Feeling or sensation — produced by Vedaniya karma. Can be pleasant (Sata) or painful (Asata). Determined by the fruit of karmic actions.
Vow or sacred commitment. The Mahavratas (great vows) for monks and Anuvratas (small vows) for laypersons.
Activity of mind, speech, and body. In Jainism, Yoga is the cause of karmic influx (Asrava) because it generates vibrations that attract karmic matter.
